items.quote: ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

The ideal gas entropy can be rigorously derived using statistical mechanics and depends on the degrees of freedom of the molecule. The greatest contributions to the gas-phase entropy are typically from the translational and rotational modes, which under isothermal conditions primarily depend on the system volume and principle moments of inertia of the molecule, respectively. Considering that adsorption limits the accessible volume and potentially hinders the rotational freedom of a molecule, it is conceivable that the entropy of adsorption may be predicted by using geometric arguments. For example, Denayer et al. have demonstrated that the driving force behind the zeolitic separation of alkane/isoalkane mixtures is exclusively the difference in rotational loss, represented by a ratio between the molecule's radius of gyration and the cavity's largest inscribed van der Waals radius. $ ^{26} $ De Moor et al. $ ^{27} $ used ab initio simulations to show that the adsorption entropies for n-alkanes within acidic zeolites are linearly correlated with their carbon number. Specifically, our results show that adsorbed and gas-phase entropies are linearly correlated; however, the slope of this correlation has a nonlinear relationship with framework metrics (e.g., occupiable volume and limiting pore diameter). items.quote: ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). items.quote: Developing such predictive relationships would enable (1) rapid screening of zeolites for various applications, e.g., separation of hydrocarbon or oxygenate mixtures and confinement-driven reactions (as discussed briefly later) and (2) eliciting the important descriptors of molecular adsorption in microporous materials and the nature of their influence on thermodynamic quantities. In this context, here, we develop data-driven thermodynamic models to predict entropy of adsorption ( $ \Delta S_{ads} $), isosteric heat ( $ Q_{st} $), and Henry's adsorption constant ( $ K_{H} $) from molecular and zeolite structural information. To train these models, we build on our previous work $ ^{10} $ to compute these thermodynamic quantities for an expanded set of 3690 molecule–zeolite system combinations covering 84 molecules (spanning 15 chemical categories) and 96 pure-silica zeolite frameworks. Such a large and diverse combination of molecules and zeolites has not been considered before and enables us to build robust predictive models and gain new physical insights. Specifically, our results show that adsorbed and gas-phase entropies are linearly correlated; however, the slope of this correlation has a nonlinear relationship with framework metrics (e.g., occupiable volume and limiting pore diameter). On the other hand, a feed-forward neural network (NN) model built on a set of simple geometric descriptors of the adsorbate and the zeolite can accurately capture this nonlinearity and predict all three thermodynamic quantities. Further, to understand which molecular and zeolite descriptors contribute most to adsorption properties, i.e., to explain the NN, we leveraged a game-theoretic concept, viz., Shapley values, to deconvolute and quantify the contribution of each descriptor to the model prediction. We show that by analyzing Shapley values for specific molecule–zeolite systems, we can identify locally important descriptors for that and similar host–guest combinations; on the other hand, analysis of Shapley values across the material space allowed us to identify globally important descriptors for molecular adsorption.

items.quote: The calculation of water entropies was accomplished using an in-house build of the quasi-harmonic 2-phase theory (2PT) algorithm developed by Lin, Blanco, Pascal, Maiti, and Goddard $ ^{[17-19]} $. We have previously applied this method to estimate differences in the entropy of adsorption for reactive intermediates for ethanol dehydration $ ^{[5]} $ and acetonitrile $ ^{[6]} $ in zeolite Beta. Our implementation is described below. Periodic trajectory files from VASP are converted into the .XYZ file format using the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE) $ ^{[20]} $ with the zeolite framework atoms removed. The trajectories are unwrapped across periodic boundary conditions and sorted by water molecule to infer molecular identity using the molecular dynamics toolbox TRAVIS $ ^{[21]} $. From there, an in-house implementation of the 2PT theory is performed which includes decomposition of the molecular degrees of freedom into center of mass translation, rotation, and vibration. These are then individually passed through a Fourier transform filter and smoothed using a Savitzky-Golay filter producing Velocity Density of State (VDOS) functions for the translational, vibrational, and rotational modes.

items.quote: The entropy of adsorbates was calculated using a two-phase thermodynamic model, which decomposes molecular trajectories into their translational, rotational, and vibrational degrees of freedom, expressed as the vibrational density of states (VDOS). Each VDOS was decomposed into its gaseous and solid components according to the original algorithm $ ^{58-60} $ and integrated to obtain entropies accounting for the plasticity of the BEA framework, as previously applied in the BEA framework for ethanol dehydration. The TRAVIS molecular trajectory code was used to analyze the calculated trajectories. $ ^{61} $ Estimates of the entropy loss upon physisorption involved calculating the principal root-mean-square fluctuations of CD $ _{3} $CN from the AIMD trajectories. $ ^{62} $ Thus the entropy loss upon physisorption is predominantly caused by reduction in the translational degrees of freedom. The entropies of adsorption of CD $ _{3} $CN on Ti and (SiOH) $ _{4} $ defects were calculated as the differential changes in translational, rotational, and vibrational degrees of freedom relative to those calculated for the physisorbed state. This approach was necessary due to the difficulty in a direct AIMD method that describes absolute adsorption onto these sites from the gas phase. This, in part, may be due to the long time scales required to fully sample the relative translational and rotational modes available to gas-phase species. Thus, on Ti and (SiOH) $ _{4} $ defects, the entropy change is modified by the nonrigid modes calculated by AIMD as compared with the nonrigid modes for physisorption, including the root-mean-square fluctuations.

With cylindrical channels of a smaller diameter (0.56 nm), the MFI zeolite presents lower adsorption enthalpies and entropies. According to quantum sieving theory, this zeolite should be more selective for D₂, at least at low filling where the theory is valid. Surprisingly, the selectivity is the same as for FAU (Fig. 5). items.quote: The enthalpy and the entropy contributions to the Gibbs free energies were calculated at T = 298 K and partial pressure of 1 atm (101325 Pa). The enthalpy (H) of gas-phase pyridine and acetonitrile molecules is defined as the sum of total electronic energy ( $ E_{el} $), internal vibrational energy ( $ E_{v} $), zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE), as well as the rotational and translational contributions to the internal energy: $ H = E_{el} + E_{v} + ZPVE + E_{R} + E_{t} $. The corresponding calculated entropies (S) includes translational, ( $ S_{t} $) vibrational, ( $ S_{v} $) and rotational ( $ S_{r} $) degrees of freedom: $ S = S_{t} + S_{v} + S_{r} $. All the considered systems are in singlet state, thus the electronic contribution to the entropy is zero. Since both adsorbed molecules are constrained in the zeolite cavity their entropy contributions in the adsorption complexes were corrected as follows: the translational and rotational degrees of freedom were reduced by 1 and 1.28 [37]. The Gibbs free energies of the zeolite support consist of only vibrational and electronic contributions. The expressions of all enthalpy and entropy contributions can be found in Ref. [38].

Detailed analysis of the positive correlation observed between CO adsorption enthalpy and entropy is beyond the scope of this article. However, it seems pertinent to point out that such a positive correlation, also termed entropy–enthalpy compensation, $ ^{[22-24]} $ is widely reported to occur in a large variety of chemical processes involving weak interactions, including hydrogen bonding, $ ^{[25,26]} $ formation of weakly associated (van der Waals) molecular complexes $ ^{[27]} $ and hydrogen adsorption on zeolites. $ ^{[28]} $ When corresponding values of $ \Delta H^0 $ and $ \Delta S^0 $ cover only a small range, approximately linear plots are usually obtained, but concave curves similar to that shown in Figure 5 have also been reported in the literature $ ^{[22,23,28,29]} $ for several molecular association and adsorption processes. In general terms, for the case of carbon monoxide adsorption entropy–enthalpy compensation reflects the fact that a stronger (enthalpy related) interaction between CO and the adsorbing centre leads to a greater decrease of its motion freedom (which is related to entropy). However, there is an intrinsic limit to $ \Delta S^0 $ in the adsorption process, because the CO molecule cannot lose more than all of its degrees of translational and rotational freedom, while in principle no definite limit exists for $ \Delta H^0 $. This is likely to be the reason for the increasing slope of the $ \Delta H^0 $ against $ \Delta S^0 $ plot (Figure 5) at relatively large $ \Delta S^0 $ values.

The framework descriptor Shapley values demonstrated much greater variability compared with the adsorbate descriptors, as reflected in Figure 11. In particular, lsd_p can contribute between -0.07 and +0.07 (i.e., it can reduce or increase the fraction of entropy retained relative to gas phase by up to 7%), lsd_f can contribute between -0.15 and +0.06, density can contribute between -0.08 and +0.06, and ASA can contribute between -0.09 and +0.03. Among the framework features, lsd_f exhibits the strongest variation in Shapley values, suggesting that it is most influential in predicting the entropy ratio. These trends can be largely rationalized based on geometric arguments related to confinement. The negative trend with respect to the density feature can be explained by its inverse correlation with framework size. A larger density of sites in a zeolite usually corresponds to smaller pore sizes or reduced occupiable volume, which increases confinement and thereby reduces the fraction of retained entropy. We point the reader to Figure S11 for a heatmap of the feature correlation matrix. In contrast, the largest spherical diameter that can be included along a free path (lsd_p) and the largest free sphere (lsd_f) show positive trends between the Shapley value and their respective feature value. Large lsd_f or lsd_p values generally result in greater retention of entropy among the adsorbate due to the presence of large cages, bearing voids where the adsorbate retains translational and potentially rotational freedom. We emphasize that a small lsd_f or lsd_p does not exclusively guarantee a small entropy ratio; rather, a combination among the framework features is the best predictor. In particular, for frameworks with especially small lsd_f (<2 [Å]), we find that on average, more entropy is retained among the adsorbates than within larger lsd_f frameworks (consider Figure S12). This phenomenon suggests the presence of "ink bottle"-shaped pores, where the channels connecting the larger pores of the framework are smaller and entropically less favorable than the cages that precede them. The U-shaped trend within Figure 12M for small lsd_f (<2 [Å]) is therefore explained as small adsorbates exclusively fitting within small frameworks and consequently those systems exhibiting larger surviving entropies than their presence within larger lsd_f frameworks.

This decrease in entropy upon transition state formation is likely caused by the loss of frustrated rotational and quasi-translational degrees of freedom present in noncovalently adsorbed species confined within zeolite catalysts . $ ^ { 50 , 109 } $ The apparent enthalpic activation barrier $(\Delta H_{\mathrm{app}})$ is about 7 kJ mol$^{-1}$ smaller on Sn-Beta-F than Sn-Beta-OH (Table 2), while both catalysts exhibit a similar entropy of activation ($~\sim$148 J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$). These differences in activation parameters reflect apparent activation free energy barriers that are $\sim$7 kJ mol$^{-1}$ (evaluated at 373 K) lower on Sn-Beta-F than on Sn-Beta-OH, which give rise to zero-order rate constants that are $\sim$10× larger on Sn-Beta-F(302) than on Sn-Beta-OH(326) (Figure 3). The framework descriptor Shapley values demonstrated much greater variability compared with the adsorbate descriptors, as reflected in Figure 11. In particular, lsd_p can contribute between -0.07 and +0.07 (i.e., it can reduce or increase the fraction of entropy retained relative to gas phase by up to 7%), lsd_f can contribute between -0.15 and +0.06, density can contribute between -0.08 and +0.06, and ASA can contribute between -0.09 and +0.03. Among the framework features, lsd_f exhibits the strongest variation in Shapley values, suggesting that it is most influential in predicting the entropy ratio. These trends can be largely rationalized based on geometric arguments related to confinement. The negative trend with respect to the density feature can be explained by its inverse correlation with framework size. A larger density of sites in a zeolite usually corresponds to smaller pore sizes or reduced occupiable volume, which increases confinement and thereby reduces the fraction of retained entropy. We point the reader to Figure S11 for a heatmap of the feature correlation matrix. In contrast, the largest spherical diameter that can be included along a free path (lsd_p) and the largest free sphere (lsd_f) show positive trends between the Shapley value and their respective feature value. Large lsd_f or lsd_p values generally result in greater retention of entropy among the adsorbate due to the presence of large cages, bearing voids where the adsorbate retains translational and potentially rotational freedom. We emphasize that a small lsd_f or lsd_p does not exclusively guarantee a small entropy ratio; rather, a combination among the framework features is the best predictor. In particular, for frameworks with especially small lsd_f (<2 [Å]), we find that on average, more entropy is retained among the adsorbates than within larger lsd_f frameworks (consider Figure S12). This phenomenon suggests the presence of "ink bottle"-shaped pores, where the channels connecting the larger pores of the framework are smaller and entropically less favorable than the cages that precede them. The U-shaped trend within Figure 12M for small lsd_f (<2 [Å]) is therefore explained as small adsorbates exclusively fitting within small frameworks and consequently those systems exhibiting larger surviving entropies than their presence within larger lsd_f frameworks.

items.quote: The molecular weight is a fundamental physical quantity with a presence in the statistical mechanical expression of the translational entropy for an ideal gas, as well as in the hindered/free translator entropy approximation for adsorbates within protonic zeolites. $ ^{[11,13-16]} $ Likewise, the molecular weight is also related to the number of heavy atoms (non-hydrogen) of the molecule, which has been shown to linearly correlate with the adsorption entropy of alkanes within protonic zeolites. $ ^{[27]} $ Under standard conditions, the translational entropy is the most significant contribution toward the absolute entropy of a molecule and predictably experiences the most significant loss upon adsorption. The rotational moments of inertia make for excellent descriptors toward distinguishing among spherical, linear, and nonlinear adsorbates. Namely, molecules represented by a single sphere exhibit no rotational inertia, while linear and nonlinear molecules rotate about two and three axes, respectively. Collectively, the principle moments provide additional information about the shape of the molecule. For example, the ratio of the principle moments (i.e., $ I_1/I_3 $ and $ I_2/I_3 $) describes the molecule as being “rod-like”, “sphere-like”, “disc-like”, or “envelope-like”.⁵¹,⁵² More complicated expressions can also be derived and presumably learned by a NN model, such as the “molecular eccentricity”,⁵³ “inertial shape factor”,⁵² and “sphericity index”,⁵⁴ each of which provide additional information about the shape of the molecule. The rotational freedom of a molecule is generally the second largest contributor to the standard ideal-gas entropy of the adsorbate, and the principle moments of inertia are explicitly present in the rotational entropy equation. The principle moments are also found within the hindered/free rotor approximation for alkanes within protonic zeolites and organic molecules on two-dimensional catalytic surfaces.¹¹,⁵⁵,⁵⁶

items.quote: We performed additional analysis of the influence of zeolite confinement on the internal entropy of NH₃ desorbed from a ZCu site. As shown in Figure 6c, at r = 5.0, the principle rotational axis of NH₃ sweeps out a uniform sphere during the course of the trajectory. Sₐₜₒₜ computed from the averaged principal moments of inertia (Iₓᵣᵧᵣ) from the AIMD trajectory is 54 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, identical to the ideal gas Sₐₜₒₜ 54 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ computed from Iₓᵣᵧᵣ from an isolated NH₃. Similarly, Sᵣᵧᵣ computed from an isolated NH₃ (2.42 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) is the same as that computed for an NH₃ at the center of the zeolite cage (2.28 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Finally, the thermal wavelength of NH₃ at 473 K is 0.195 Å, smaller than the CHA cage dimensions of approximately 10 Å, so that quantum size effects are not important for Sₐₜₒₜ. We conclude that adsorbates of the dimension of NH₃ are ideal-gas-like in the fully desorbed state. To apply the PMF method to larger adsorbates, an additional correction would be necessary to account for internal entropy differences between the desorbed and external reservoir states.

The framework descriptor Shapley values demonstrated much greater variability compared with the adsorbate descriptors, as reflected in Figure 11. In particular, lsd_p can contribute between -0.07 and +0.07 (i.e., it can reduce or increase the fraction of entropy retained relative to gas phase by up to 7%), lsd_f can contribute between -0.15 and +0.06, density can contribute between -0.08 and +0.06, and ASA can contribute between -0.09 and +0.03. Among the framework features, lsd_f exhibits the strongest variation in Shapley values, suggesting that it is most influential in predicting the entropy ratio. These trends can be largely rationalized based on geometric arguments related to confinement. The negative trend with respect to the density feature can be explained by its inverse correlation with framework size. A larger density of sites in a zeolite usually corresponds to smaller pore sizes or reduced occupiable volume, which increases confinement and thereby reduces the fraction of retained entropy. We point the reader to Figure S11 for a heatmap of the feature correlation matrix. In contrast, the largest spherical diameter that can be included along a free path (lsd_p) and the largest free sphere (lsd_f) show positive trends between the Shapley value and their respective feature value. Large lsd_f or lsd_p values generally result in greater retention of entropy among the adsorbate due to the presence of large cages, bearing voids where the adsorbate retains translational and potentially rotational freedom. We emphasize that a small lsd_f or lsd_p does not exclusively guarantee a small entropy ratio; rather, a combination among the framework features is the best predictor. In particular, for frameworks with especially small lsd_f (<2 [Å]), we find that on average, more entropy is retained among the adsorbates than within larger lsd_f frameworks (consider Figure S12). This phenomenon suggests the presence of "ink bottle"-shaped pores, where the channels connecting the larger pores of the framework are smaller and entropically less favorable than the cages that precede them. The U-shaped trend within Figure 12M for small lsd_f (<2 [Å]) is therefore explained as small adsorbates exclusively fitting within small frameworks and consequently those systems exhibiting larger surviving entropies than their presence within larger lsd_f frameworks.
